doc.title: Phil Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 27, 2023

title: Lennie Johnson and the Quincy Jones band trumpet section
summary: Lennie Johnson taught Wilson and Bill Chase at Berklee, played lead for Basie and Quincy Jones; they recall the Free and Easy trumpet section and Floyd Standifer.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: 284 Newbury Street, it’s a brown house — that’s the Berklee School of Music and there’s no degree given out. You can get a diploma. And all of a sudden you have teachers like Lennie Johnson — Lennie Johnson was a lead trumpet player you probably never heard of, but when Cat Anderson got shall we say, took a vacation to get his head back together, Lennie Johnson went out and covered for him for six weeks. And this was a regular happening over and over. So that in itself was a family. Lennie taught Bill Chase and myself at Berklee in 1955. I was supposedly at New England but ten blocks away was this Berklee School of Music and I wasn’t allowed to go to because it didn’t have a degree. My father being an academic in the Ivy League you know said, “No degree? You can’t go there.” So ten blocks away though was the Berklee School of Music and that’s really where I was. Because they always needed trombone players. It was like a factory for big bands you know, they were all over the place. And so Chase and I learned to lock in on each other. As a lead player I’d be playing lead trombone, he’d be playing lead trumpet beautifully, just, you know, and he played lead trumpet beautifully largely because of Lennie Johnson’s influence. Basie’s band had the same thing he would go play lead with Basie’s band and I played with Lennie at all of the Italian clubs around Boston and you know the big — Sinatra would come in and all that sort of stuff. So boy what we learned off Lennie. And he was a simple man who was extremely talented. He also went and played lead for Quincy Jones in that first Quincy Jones band that went overseas with Sarah Vaughan.
Oh the Free and Easy Band.
Yeah. I know I have a picture of that, I’ll have to look, yeah.
Well I had two — I’ll get some names wrong here — but that trumpet section they tell me was —

Clark Terry, Benny Bailey, Lennie Johnson, and Larry, another lead player. I think his first name was Larry. He was awesome. And then Floyd Standifer my dear friend. Floyd Standifer you’ve never heard of.

Another educator out of Olympia, Washington. That’s where he was raised. And he was with Quincy Jones’s band and there’s Clark and Benny and Lennie and X I can’t come up with the name, and then Floyd Standifer and none of these guys knew Floyd Standifer. He said he had one solo a night. It was on the bridge of “Cherokee.” And he said it took him eight bars to get it down to the microphone and eight bars —
The things you don’t learn in school.
